title: Bengaluru Startup Unveils PRAGYA, India's First Private Fusion Tokamak
excerpt: Pranos Fusion built the compact experimental reactor in eight months on a fraction of global fusion budgets, giving India a homegrown testbed for plasma research — though commercial fusion power remains years away.
body:
• Bengaluru startup Pranos Fusion has completed PRAGYA, described as India's first privately developed tokamak — a compact experimental machine for creating and controlling plasma.
  • Built in about eight months by a 12-member team working with JNCASR and IISc, PRAGYA is a testbed, not a power plant: it does not produce fusion energy or net energy gain.
  • Pranos raised $6.8 million (about ₹63 crore) in March 2026 — a fraction of the billions spent on government-led fusion programmes worldwide.
  • The company aims to work toward a full-scale 50–100 MW fusion reactor around 2030, an ambitious target that depends on years of disciplined validation.

PRAGYA: India's first privately built tokamak

India has a new "artificial sun" — and this one was built by a startup, not the government. Bengaluru-based Pranos Fusion has completed PRAGYA, a compact tokamak that uses powerful magnetic fields to confine superheated plasma — the state of matter in which fusion happens. The machine, roughly four feet across, is described as India's first privately developed tokamak, moving the country's private fusion story from design documents to working hardware.

A tokamak is a doughnut-shaped device at the heart of most fusion research: its ring-shaped vacuum chamber magnetically confines plasma — a hot gas of free electrons and ions — so the particles spiral inside, collide and, under extreme conditions, fuse and release energy. It is the process that powers the sun. PRAGYA's plasma chamber has a radius of just 40 cm; by comparison, the tokamak at the multinational ITER project in France has a radius of 6.2 m, according to the Hindu BusinessLine.

Context & Background

Fusion has been India's public-sector pursuit for decades. The Institute for Plasma Research (IPR) in Gandhinagar operates ADITYA-1, ADITYA-U and SST-1 — the last notable for using superconducting magnets — and India is a partner in the ITER project in France. IPR recently commissioned India's first spherical tokamak, achieving first plasma on December 11, 2025 and running 114 plasma discharges since, the Hindu BusinessLine reported.

Pranos Fusion, founded in 2024 by physicist Dr Shaurya Kaushal and Roshan George, took a different route. The company began with JENGA, software for computing optimal tokamak designs, and started building PRAGYA in June 2025. In March 2026, researchers from Pranos, JNCASR and the Indian Institute of Science published a peer-reviewed paper detailing the design of PRAGYA's vacuum vessel. The machine was assembled in about eight months by a 12-member team of physicists, engineers and computational scientists at JNCASR's Innovation and Development Centre.

"This is a small, compact tokamak designed as a precursor to a larger tokamak, with scientific exploration and development of critical human resources as a core objective."

— Shaurya Kaushal, co-founder, Pranos Fusion, in a joint research paper

Impact & Analysis

The significance of PRAGYA is not a physics breakthrough — the company is clear the machine cannot conduct nuclear fusion at this stage — but speed and cost. Pranos raised $6.8 million (about ₹63 crore) in March 2026 in a round co-led by pi Ventures and Ankur Capital, with participation from Industrial47 and angel investors. That is a microscopic fraction of the billions poured into ITER and other national programmes. It is designed to run up to 3,000 plasma shots a year — roughly 10 to 12 experiments a day — and the company plans to operate it for nearly two decades.

Pranos is developing three connected layers: JENGA design software, PRAGYA as the experimental testbed, and MAGGA, high-temperature superconducting magnets that could shrink future reactors. The caveats are real. The company still faces supply-chain bottlenecks for specialized components, a shortage of trained fusion personnel, and the long-term question of tritium supply, as researcher Animesh Ghosh told India Today earlier this year.

Diaspora Angle

For the diaspora, PRAGYA is a familiar Indian story told in a new domain: frugal engineering aimed at a frontier problem. The model will be familiar to NRIs in deep tech: build talent, suppliers and testing infrastructure at home rather than waiting for the technology to mature abroad. It also creates a two-way street: diaspora scientists and engineers with overseas lab and startup experience have skills this sector now needs.

What's Next

Pranos says its longer-term ambition is a full-scale fusion reactor capable of producing 50–100 MW of electricity around 2030 — an ambitious goal, not a delivery date. Before that comes years of disciplined validation: plasma stability studies, magnet development, heating tests and repeatable plasma experiments on PRAGYA. On the public side, IPR's spherical tokamak team continues working on plasma stability and wall conditioning. If either track sustains momentum, India will have built a fusion pipeline that runs on startup speed as well as state scale.
